Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Priya was twenty-two and working as a delivery driver for a regional courier service when she was mugged one evening in a strip-mall parking lot. A man approached her as she unlocked her car, told her to hand over her wallet and phone, and pressed something hard against her ribs. She complied instantly, frozen. The man fled, and she stood there for a long moment before calling the police. When they arrived, she could barely speak; she kept thinking she should have done something—shouted, run, fought back. That feeling of having been forced into helpless obedience lodged itself inside her, and the image of the man’s hand on her shoulder remained as a single snapshot that replayed without warning.

In the weeks that followed, Priya became acutely sensitive to any situation where she felt pressured or controlled. Being told what to do by a manager, or even having a customer hurry her, sent a spike of alarm through her chest. This loss of autonomy was her most potent trigger. She also began to react to the presence of authority figures: seeing a police car in her rearview mirror made her heart race, even when she had done nothing wrong. And she started scanning crowds for people who looked suspicious—anyone loitering, anyone who made eye contact a second too long. Each perceived threat ignited not only fear but also an involuntary return to that parking lot moment. Sometimes she would hear the man’s low voice in her head, a fragment of auditory recall layered over an emotion so intense that her body reacted before her mind caught up.

These triggers drove her maladaptive strategies. To avoid the feeling of being forced into submission, she began refusing deliveries to unfamiliar addresses and eventually stopped driving altogether. She told herself the robbery was not that bad, that she was overreacting, a form of magical thinking that let her push the memory away for a few hours. At night, when she could not relax and woke repeatedly to check her locks, she smoked marijuana to dull the hypervigilance. The escape route planning she did before entering any building—scanning exits, noting escape paths—only reinforced her sense that danger was everywhere, and that isolation was safer than being with others who might not understand. Her inaction guilt was relentless: she could not forgive herself for not fighting back, and this self-blame made her more likely to avoid driving, because every time she got behind the wheel she replayed her inaction and felt the shame all over again. The helplessness she now carried—a conviction that she could not stop bad things from happening—deepened her threat perception, making her perpetually alert for signs of coercion or hostility.

Over the months, the vicious cycles tightened. Memory triggered threat: whenever the auditory recall surfaced, she would wake in the night to check the apartment. Threat then amplified negative appraisals: her constant scanning made her feel isolated, set apart from friends who could relax. The threat also generated new triggers—her hyperawareness of suspicious behavior made her see suspicious behavior everywhere, feeding the loop. In turn, her maladaptive strategies, especially avoidance of driving, made her more dependent on family for rides, which meant more authority figures telling her what to do, which triggered her again. She began using marijuana heavily to numb the guilt and the 4 a.m. replays, but the drug use also left her groggy and more vulnerable to perceiving threats in ordinary sounds.

What finally brought Priya to a clinic was a near-collision: she had driven for the first time in two months to attend a family dinner, saw a police car, panicked, ran a red light, and barely avoided an accident. She now fears that her own mind is conspiring against her—that she will never feel safe again, that she will always be trapped by the moment she did nothing. What she hopes for, quietly, is to be able to deliver a single package without needing to map three exits first.
